title: Strategic Partner Leads and GRDC Q&A
text:
Summary
Join us for a closing panel discussion with AAGI’s strategic partner leads and a representative from the Grains Research and Development Corporation (GRDC). Chaired by Nathan O’Callaghan, the panel will reflect on what AAGI has achieved, the opportunities and challenges ahead, and how the partnership can continue to deliver value for the Australian grains industry.
This is your opportunity to put questions directly to the panel. You can submit your questions throughout the Symposium using the GroupMap link via the QR code. 
We are particularly interested in questions that look ahead, such as where AAGI should focus next, how analytics can deliver greater value to growers and the Australian grains industry, what capabilities and ways of working we will need, and how AAGI can continue to be a strong avenue to study and build a career. The most useful questions will be relevant to the whole room and draw on the panel’s collective perspective, rather than focusing on an individual project or personal circumstance.
Submitted questions will be reviewed before the session, and similar questions may be combined. We may not be able to put every question to the panel, but all contributions will help shape the discussion.
The session will be followed by an awards ceremony, celebrating the best poster and the best 3-minute pitch from the poster session.
Scan the GroupMap QR code to submit questions that will be answered during this session. The link also lets you vote for the best 3-minute pitch and the best poster.

title: Posters
text:
Poster Guidelines
We encourage all AAGI Symposium participants to prepare a poster showcasing their research, project, tools, or area of work. The poster session provides an opportunity to share ideas, highlight your work, and foster discussion and collaboration across the AAGI community.

Poster Templates
The AAGI poster templates can be downloaded from this Box folder:
AAGI Poster Templates ↗


Poster Content
Posters should clearly communicate:

The research, project, tool, or area of work being presented.
The problem, question, or objective being addressed.
The methods, approach, or workflow used.
Key findings, outcomes, or expected impacts (where available).
Contact details to enable follow-up discussions and collaboration.



Poster Format

Size: A0 (841 × 1189 mm)
Orientation: Portrait

Posters will be displayed on double-sided poster boards, with two A0 portrait posters displayed on each side.


QR Code
Please include a QR code placeholder on your poster. This will be used to link to the digital version of your poster on the symposium website. A minimum size of 8 × 8 cm is recommended to ensure the QR code can be scanned easily.


File Requirements

Format: PDF
File name: Please use the following format: Poster_SurnameFirstName.pdf

Example: Poster_SmithJohn.pdf

Number of posters: One poster per participant. Collaborative group posters are encouraged where a project has multiple contributors.





Poster Submission
Submission deadline: 25 October 2026
This deadline allows sufficient time for posters to be printed in Perth and ensures they are ready for display at the symposium.


Submission Process
Poster submission involves two steps:
1. Complete the Google Form
The Google form collects your poster details and a few questions about the poster showcase. A confirmation email will be sent to the email address you provide.
Submit Your Poster Details ↗
2. Upload your poster to Box
Use the Box link to upload your PDF poster. You do not need a Box account to upload a file.
Upload Your Poster ↗

title: Workshop 1AI in AAGI: From Tools to Workflows
text:
Summary
Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming scientific research, creating new opportunities for knowledge discovery, data analysis, and computational tool development. This workshop will showcase major trends shaping the current AI landscape, exploring how emerging technologies are changing research practices and how they can be adopted effectively and responsibly. Through a series of presentations, we will examine AI-assisted literature exploration and research gap identification, AI-driven tool development, and the growing role of locally deployed AI models in supporting research workflows. Attention will be given to responsible AI practices, including the generation and use of synthetic data, management of sensitive research datasets, data privacy, and research integrity. Bringing together practical applications, emerging technologies and responsible data management strategies, the workshop aims to provide researchers with a broader understanding of AI’s evolving role in science, encourage knowledge sharing across AAGI, and identify opportunities for collaboration and innovation in the Australian grains research community.

Summary
This workshop will showcase how modern computational approaches are shaping genomic and omics research. It will begin with a focus on Trusted Research Environments (TREs) and federated analytics and learning in omics, highlighting how secure and controlled research environments can support the analysis and sharing of sensitive or distributed data while enabling collaboration across institutions. The workshop will also highlight reproducible workflows, computational approaches and tools being developed and applied across different areas of bioinformatics, providing an opportunity to share expertise, build connections and explore future opportunities for collaboration across AAGI.

title: Workshop 2Efficient Trial Design with speed
text:
Summary
speed is an R package from AAGI-AU that generates spatially optimised, model-free experimental designs. In this hands-on workshop, we’ll explain what model-free means in practice, give a conceptual overview of how speed works, then walk through:

Standard designs such as RCBD and split-plot
Row-column, p-rep, and multi-environment trial (MET) designs
Incorporating a relationship matrix or covariates
Writing your own objective functions

Participants should be comfortable in R.
Please bring a laptop with speed installed:
if (!require("pak", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("biometryhub/speed")

Summary
The Higher Degree by Research (HDR) student and Early Career Researchers (ECR) session brings together HDR students and early career researchers from across AAGI for a panel and interactive Q&A. title: WUR WorkshopLMMs, AI and ODEs for G×E
text:
Summary
This workshop presents modern statistical and computational approaches for analysing and predicting genotype-by-environment (G×E) interactions in plant breeding. It covers mixed model splines and random regression for spatial, temporal and environmental data; kernel-based mixed models and AI approaches for G×E; and the integration of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) with physics-informed neural networks for crop modelling.

title: WUR WorkshopLMMs, AI and ODEs for G×E
text:
Programme

09:00 - 10:30 | Mixed model splines and random regression for spatio-temporal data and G×E
Modern plant breeding experiments increasingly generate complex data from field trials, sensor platforms, drones, satellites, and controlled-environment phenotyping systems. These data often exhibit spatial and temporal structure that must be accounted for to obtain reliable estimates of genetic effects and genotype-by-environment interactions (G×E). Linear mixed models provide a powerful framework for analysing such data, while extensions based on splines and random regression offer flexible tools for modelling smooth trends across space, time, and environmental gradients.
Mixed model splines combine the flexibility of nonparametric smoothing with the statistical rigor and computational efficiency of mixed models. They can be used to separate systematic spatial and temporal variation from genetic effects, enabling improved correction of field trials and the analysis of complex multidimensional phenotyping data. Functional data approaches further extend this framework by modelling complete trajectories of traits measured over time and summarising biological responses through functional principal components.
For the analysis and prediction of G×E, random regression models provide a flexible approach to describe genotype-specific responses to environmental covariates. Reduced-rank formulations allow the simultaneous analysis of multiple environmental variables while maintaining computational feasibility for large breeding datasets. These models can be used not only to estimate genotype responses in observed environments but also to predict performance in new environments and quantify the associated uncertainty.
Presentations

Martin Boer: Multidimensional mixed model splines for spatial field trials and high-throughput phenotyping data, demonstrated with the R package LMMsolver.
Junita Solin: Spline-based functional models and functional principal component analysis for longitudinal photosynthesis measurements in Arabidopsis and their relationship with biomass accumulation.
Jip Ramakers: Reduced-rank random regression models for G×E analysis and prediction using multi-environment wheat trial data.



11:00 - 13:00 | Kernels and AI for modelling genotype-by-environment interactions
Estimating and predicting the performance of varieties across diverse environments is one of the central challenges in modern plant breeding. As breeding programs increasingly rely on sparse and large-scale multi-environment trials, there is a growing need for modelling frameworks that can efficiently capture complex genotype-by-environment (G×E) interactions while retaining predictive accuracy. Recent developments in kernel methods, high-performance computing, and artificial intelligence are opening new opportunities to address these challenges.
Kernel-based mixed models provide a flexible framework for modelling genetic, environmental, and management-related sources of variation, including higher-order interaction effects such as G×E×M. By representing relationships between genotypes and environments through kernels, these models can accommodate complex patterns of covariance while remaining compatible with standard mixed model software and REML-based parameter estimation. At the same time, advances in computing technology are making it possible to fit increasingly large and complex mixed models through GPU-accelerated algorithms and datacenter-scale hardware.
Artificial intelligence and deep-learning approaches offer complementary opportunities for predicting crop performance from high-dimensional genetic and environmental information. By combining neural networks with mixed model concepts, hybrid approaches seek to exploit the strengths of both methodologies: the predictive flexibility of machine learning and the interpretability and statistical structure of mixed models.
Presentations

Killian Melsen: A kernel-based linear mixed model framework for modelling G×E and G×E×M interactions, and recent GPU/CPU implementations of REML estimation for large-scale datasets.
Aike Potze: MixINN, a framework combining mixed models and neural networks to predict crop performance from genetic and environmental information, with practical demonstrations using PyTorch-based interactive notebooks.



14:00 - 15:30 | ODE-based crop modelling
Crop traits like yield and resilience are complex breeding targets. The prediction of these traits likely improves when accounting for time-dynamic G×E interactions over the growing season. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) are hybrid models that combine time-dynamic neural networks like LSTMs or GRUs with ordinary differential equations (ODEs). ODEs explicitly link the development rate of crop traits to the current state of the crop and its interactions with its environment, allowing for an evaluation of those traits at any time point. Function rules codify biological assumptions about limitations following from different variables, like light, temperature, soil water, or nitrogen. Model parameters are taken as genotype dependent. The ODEs are implemented in software for time-integration and fitting to time series data of monitored crop traits to optimize parameters. The ODEs are then merged with PINNs implemented in PyTorch or Torch for R, where they function as (biologically informed) penalty term for model training. Ideally, these trained PINNs improve predictions of how different genotypes will perform in new environments. Challenges include dealing with equifinality, parameter and model identification, and over-fitting.
Presentations

Neil Budko: Fundamentals of ODE-based models.
George van Voorn: ODE-based crop models and their integration with PINNs.
Corné Verburg: Identification of ODE functions from observational data using the SINDY algorithm.

title: Bioinformatics Satellite MeetingApplied Bioinformatics: Emerging Tools and Data-Driven Approaches in Crop Research
text:
Summary
Advances in bioinformatics, genomics and machine learning are transforming how we investigate crop genetic diversity, understand plant-pathogen interactions and improve agricultural traits. This workshop will showcase emerging computational approaches and their practical applications in crop research, bringing together researchers from across AAGI and collaborating institutions. Presentations will explore recent developments in graph pangenomics, gene presence–absence variation, structural variation analysis and genomic visualisation, alongside machine learning approaches for variant discovery, trait prediction, genomic selection and crop image analysis. The programme will also highlight advances in multi-omics integration, AI-driven protein–protein interaction prediction, and large language models for scientific literature mining and knowledge curation. Through a combination of methodological developments and applied research case studies, the workshop aims to demonstrate how computational technologies are helping researchers extract biological insights from increasingly complex datasets, address challenges in crop improvement and disease resistance, and encourage knowledge exchange and collaboration across the grains research community. The event is open to all AAGI members and associates, particularly those involved in managing, analysing or interpreting crop research data, regardless of their bioinformatics background.
